pages.text: It was early on a summer morning, and the beach was almost empty. The sand was still cool. The sea was wavy, with white tops on the waves. Miriam and her dad were playing ball by the water. It was her favourite ball, striped like a sweet.
pages.speech: It was early on a summer morning, and the beach was almost empty. The sand was still cool. The sea was wavy, with white tops on the waves. Miriam and her dad were playing ball by the water. It was her favourite ball, striped like a sweet.

pages.text: Throw, catch. Throw, catch. The wind tugged at the ball as it flew. Up on the sand stood the lifeguard tower, with a big chair at the top. The chair was empty. The lifeguard had not arrived yet.
pages.speech: Throw, catch. Throw, catch. The wind tugged at the ball as it flew. Up on the sand stood the lifeguard tower, with a big chair at the top. The chair was empty. The lifeguard had not arrived yet.

pages.text: Dad threw the ball high. Miriam reached up, but a gust of wind lifted it right over her hands. It bounced once on the wet sand, rolled into the foam and floated. “My ball!” cried Miriam.
pages.speech: Dad threw the ball high. Miriam reached up, but a gust of wind lifted it right over her hands. It bounced once on the wet sand, rolled into the foam and floated. “My ball!” cried Miriam.

pages.text: A wave lifted the ball and carried it out. Then another wave carried it a little farther. The ball bobbed up and down, bright against the grey-green water, farther and farther from the shore.
pages.speech: A wave lifted the ball and carried it out. Then another wave carried it a little farther. The ball bobbed up and down, bright against the grey-green water, farther and farther from the shore.

pages.text: Miriam ran to the edge of the water and stopped. Her toes were in the foam. The sea pulled at her ankles, then let go, then pulled again. The ball looked so close. Just a few steps, she thought. Just a few steps.
pages.speech: Miriam ran to the edge of the water and stopped. Her toes were in the foam. The sea pulled at her ankles, then let go, then pulled again. The ball looked so close. Just a few steps, she thought. Just a few steps.

pages.text: She looked at the lifeguard tower. The big chair was still empty. Nobody was watching the sea. Miriam stood very still, and the ball bobbed out, farther and farther. “Dad!” she called.
pages.speech: She looked at the lifeguard tower. The big chair was still empty. Nobody was watching the sea. Miriam stood very still, and the ball bobbed out, farther and farther. “Dad!” she called.

pages.text: Dad came and stood beside her. He looked at the ball. He looked at the waves, rolling in one after another. Then he took Miriam’s hand. “Let it go,” he said gently.
pages.speech: Dad came and stood beside her. He looked at the ball. He looked at the waves, rolling in one after another. Then he took Miriam’s hand. “Let it go,” he said gently.

pages.text: “But it’s my favourite ball,” said Miriam. Her voice wobbled. “I know,” said Dad. “The sea is stronger than it looks this morning. And you matter much more to me than any ball.” He squeezed her hand.
pages.speech: “But it’s my favourite ball,” said Miriam. Her voice wobbled. “I know,” said Dad. “The sea is stronger than it looks this morning. And you matter much more to me than any ball.” He squeezed her hand.

pages.text: They watched the ball together until it was a tiny dot, and then they could not see it at all. Miriam leaned against Dad. A tear rolled down her cheek, and the wind dried it.

pages.text: They built a sandcastle while the sun climbed higher. They dug a moat and decorated the walls with shells. Slowly the beach filled with families, umbrellas and towels. But Miriam still thought about her ball.
pages.speech: They built a sandcastle while the sun climbed higher. They dug a moat and decorated the walls with shells. Slowly the beach filled with families, umbrellas and towels. But Miriam still thought about her ball.

pages.text: Then the lifeguard arrived. Her day was only just starting, and her big chair was still empty. Before she climbed up, she came walking down the beach towards them, laughing. Under her arm was a striped ball.
pages.speech: Then the lifeguard arrived. Her day was only just starting, and her big chair was still empty. Before she climbed up, she came walking down the beach towards them, laughing. Under her arm was a striped ball.

pages.text: “Is this yours?” asked the lifeguard. “The sea washed it up right next to my tower.” Miriam hugged the ball tight. “You stayed on the sand and called your dad,” said the lifeguard. “That was exactly the right thing to do.”
pages.speech: “Is this yours?” asked the lifeguard. “The sea washed it up right next to my tower.” Miriam hugged the ball tight. “You stayed on the sand and called your dad,” said the lifeguard. “That was exactly the right thing to do.”

pages.text: Then the lifeguard climbed her tower and sat high in her chair, watching the water. Miriam and Dad went into the sea together, close to the tower, where the lifeguard could see them. The waves lifted them up and set them gently down.
pages.speech: Then the lifeguard climbed her tower and sat high in her chair, watching the water. Miriam and Dad went into the sea together, close to the tower, where the lifeguard could see them. The waves lifted them up and set them gently down.

pages.text: Miriam waved at the tower, and the lifeguard waved back. The striped ball rested safely on their towel, under Dad’s sandal, so the wind could not take it again. Miriam splashed Dad, and Dad splashed her back, right where the lifeguard could see them.

activity.title: Boat Test
activity.goal: Test how shape and weight change what floats.
materials: Kitchen foil (squares about the size of a hand)
A wide basin with a little water, a few centimetres deep
A towel, paper and a pencil

steps.caption: Fold a small boat from foil.
Guess: how many pebbles before it sinks? Write it down.
Float it. Add pebbles one at a time. Count.
Change the shape: wider, with higher sides. Try again.
Which boat carried the most? Why?

activity.safety: An adult watches the water the whole time, even when there is only a little. A few centimetres of water are enough, and the basin is emptied straight after. Foil edges can be sharp, so fold them inwards. Keep the pebbles away from toddlers, and wash hands afterwards. If there is an accident, call your local emergency number.
activity.forAdult: In the story, the waves take Miriam’s ball, and she stops at the water’s edge and calls her dad instead of chasing it. They go into the sea only after the lifeguard has arrived, and close to the tower. This is the rule on a real beach too: swim only where and when a lifeguard is on duty, and with an adult watching. Children can drown in very little water, quickly and silently. That is why even this small basin needs an adult watching it the whole time. The activity itself answers a question children love: why does one thing float and another sink? Fold a small boat together from a square of foil, turning up the edges to make sides. Before it goes in the water, ask the child to guess: “How many pebbles will it carry before it sinks?” Write the guess down. Put the boat on the water, add pebbles one at a time and count together. Then change the shape: a wider boat with a flat bottom, or one with higher sides, and try again. A wide, flat boat usually carries the most, because it pushes more water aside before it sinks. Ask: “Which boat carried the most? Why do you think so?” Praise the testing and the thinking (“you changed one thing and tried again”), not just the number of pebbles. Twenty-five minutes is about right. To make it easier, the adult folds one boat and the child adds the pebbles. To make it harder, draw a table for each shape with the guess and the result. And when the game is over, empty the basin straight away.
activity.inClass: One basin for each group of four, and one adult for every eight children, watching the water the whole time. Each child folds their own boat, and the group writes down its guesses before testing. At the end, each group shows the boat that carried the most and explains its shape.
